Wrack.et: From Middle Low German wrak, probably from Old Saxon *wrak, derived from wrekan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrekan, from Proto-Germanic *wrekaną, whence also German rächen and English wreak. Cognate with Dutch wrak, English wrack, wreck, Norwegian Bokmål vrak, …

wringen.et: Borrowed from German Low German wringen, from Middle Low German wringen, from Old Saxon wringan, from Proto-West Germanic *wringan, from Proto-Germanic *wringaną. German cognates include ringen, renken and würgen. Compare also Low German wringen, Dutch wringen…

Wrana.et: Borrowed from Czech Vrána or Slovak Vrana.

s: swede, neep, rutabaga (Brassica napus subsp. rapifera)
Wruke.et: From eastern Low German (Mecklenburg, Pomerania, West Prussia), perhaps originally meaning “knobby tree trunk”. Further origin uncertain. Occasionally used in standard German since the 18th century. Cognate with synonymous Czech brukev, Polish brukiew, Kashubi…

Wrobbel.et:
Ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *vorbьľь (“sparrow”), via:
* Polish Wróbel, from wróbel
* Lower Sorbian wrobel
* Upper Sorbian wrobl

s: Wriezen (a town in eastern Brandenburg, Germany)
Wriezen.et: From West Slavic, from *vъ- (“in”) + *rěka (“river”) + *-ьje (“place suffix”). Compare Polish Wrzecień.
